title: When rehat is broken
hookLine: breaking the code is met with a penance set by five Sikhs

lines: A WEEK OF WORDS SAID ALOUD.
THE CODE WALKS YOU TO THE FRONT.
cards: This week has been full of words said out loud: four rounds at a wedding, a prayer at the pyre, five Sikhs giving amrit, the rehat explained before anyone leaves.
Which leaves the question nobody likes to ask at a ceremony. What happens when someone breaks it? Not dramatically.

A person who promised, and meant it, slips. A rule bends, then gives. In some everyday groups, an office, a team, a family, that's handled with silence: the person drifts to the back row, then out the door.
The Sikh code takes a different road. It walks the person to the front.

teach.h: TANKHAH: THE PENANCE FOR A BREACH.
teach.b: Tankhah is the penance set for a Sikh who has broken the code; someone under it is called a tankhaiya. Here's the process in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, paraphrased.
The person goes to the nearest sangat, the gathered congregation, and stands before it in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.
There they say what they did; no one has to drag it out of them, because the code expects the person to come.
Then five Sikhs, chosen from the sangat and in good standing under the code, hear the case and decide the tankhah.

teach.h: AN ARDAS, AND IT IS CLOSED.
teach.b: The person accepts it without arguing back, and the matter closes with an ardas, the standing prayer, offered for them. Look at what that does.
First, the confession is open: owned in front of the community the promise was made to, not whispered behind a curtain. Second, the judgment is shared.
Not one elder with a grudge or a soft spot, but five, the same number that gives amrit. Welcomed in by five, set right by five. Third, there's an end.
The tankhah is set, carried out and prayed over, and the person stands again as one of the sangat; the code doesn't leave a mark on them for life.
For the gravest breaches, the four named yesterday, the person also takes amrit again after penance.
For other lapses, the tankhah itself is the road back. What the process never offers is hiding. The way home goes through the front of the room.

how: Under the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a Sikh who has broken the code confesses before the sangat in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, five Sikhs set a tankhah, and the matter closes with an ardas.

games.why: the code walks the person to the front: an open confession, a penance set by five Sikhs, and an ardas that closes it.

practice: Let one small, recent mistake come to mind, not the biggest, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence that starts with I: not they made me, not it happened, but I did this.
Then add one more sentence, what would set it right, and let the two sit side by side.
